sum: Philip Morris International faced two investor-relevant developments during the week ending Saturday, November 7, 2026. The company agreed to sell inhaled-drug specialist Vectura to Molex Asia Holdings, while a Dutch anti-smoking foundation prepared a criminal complaint over alleged IQOS marketing violations.

Pharmaphorum reported on Friday, November 6, that PMI is selling Vectura to Molex Asia Holdings for a fraction of the GBP 1.1 billion it paid for the business three years ago. Vectura develops inhaled medicines and drug-delivery technologies, so the disposal marks a retreat from an expansion beyond PMI's traditional tobacco operations.

The sale puts capital allocation and portfolio discipline back in focus. The final consideration, completion timetable and any deferred payments will determine the transaction's financial effect. The disposal also narrows PMI's diversification outside its core nicotine portfolio.

NL Times reported on Monday, November 2, that the Foundation for Youth Smoking Prevention plans to file criminal charges against Philip Morris with Dutch prosecutors. The group alleges that PMI misled consumers about the health risks of its heated-tobacco system and breached restrictions on nicotine advertising.

The planned filing is expected by mid-November. NL Times said the Dutch National Institute for Public Health and the Environment considers heated tobacco harmful and not a safe alternative to smoking. The allegations have not been established by a court, but the action could increase reputational pressure on PMI's smoke-free strategy.

Philip Morris stock faces Dutch criminal complaint over IQOS claims
sum: A Dutch anti-smoking foundation plans to submit a criminal complaint against Philip Morris in mid-November, accusing the tobacco group of misleading consumers about IQOS and violating the Netherlands' ban on nicotine-product advertising. The foundation announced the action on Monday, November 2, according to TabakNee.

The Youth Smoking Prevention Foundation says Philip Morris presents heated tobacco as a less harmful alternative to conventional cigarettes while relying mainly on company-funded studies. It alleges that the company leaves out worrying findings from independent research and has engaged in prohibited advertising for nicotine products.

The allegations have not been established by a court. Philip Morris promotes IQOS as a system that heats tobacco rather than burns it. The foundation disputes the health framing of that product strategy and argues that heated tobacco remains addictive and harmful.

The planned complaint will be handed to the Dutch Public Prosecution Service. Lawyers Bénédicte Ficq, Sjoerd Lopik and Lisette van der Linde prepared the filing, according to the foundation. The action is accompanied by the public Stop Philip M. campaign.

The Netherlands Cancer Institute, KWF Cancer Society, the Lung Fund, the Heart Foundation, the Dutch lung specialists' association NVALT, Lung Cancer Netherlands and the Dutch Journal of Medicine have said they support the complaint. The foundation says earlier fines, regulatory sanctions and settlements did not stop what it describes as continuing violations.

The campaigners also point to a previous complaint filed in 2016 against tobacco manufacturers. That case did not lead to prosecution after a court held that regulation of the tobacco industry belonged to government policy. The new action is based, in the foundation's view, on existing rules against misleading consumers and tobacco advertising.

items.t: What Would It Take For Philip Morris Stock To Do It Again?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Philip Morris International (PM) sells cigarettes such as Marlboro alongside smoke-free products such as IQOS and ZYN nicotine pouches. Its stock rose 120.3% from September 30, 2021, to October 30, 2026, before dividends. A climb like that makes it natural to credit the business for all of it. So how much of the rise do you think came from Philip Morris simply selling more?
Philip Morris generated $30.7 billion in sales over the twelve months to September 2021. Five years later, that figure had grown 40.3% to reach $43.1 billion.

Twelve-month sales rose in every one of those five years. But selling more explains only a little more than two-fifths of the stock’s 120.3% rise, calculated on a compounding basis rather than simple division.
Sales represent one of four sources of a share price, alongside the margin, the multiple investors pay and the number of shares.

Then: sales and net margin for the twelve months to Sep 30, 2021, the diluted share count for the quarter ended that day, and the multiple at the close of Sep 30, 2021. Now: the twelve months and the quarter to Sep 30, 2026, and the multiple at the close of Oct 30, 2026. The four shares add up to 100% before rounding. A negative share means that source pulled the price down. Split-adjusted share price, dividends excluded.

The price-to-earnings multiple reflects what investors pay for each dollar of profit, and it rose from 16.4 to 30.4 at the October 30, 2026, close. That single change explains more than three-quarters of the stock’s rise, marking a bigger share than sales.

5 Dividend Stocks With Fortress-Like Coverage and Room for Things to Go Wrong
sum: A fat dividend yield means nothing if the cash runs dry before the check clears. These five companies show wildly different margins of safety, and one of them barely cleared the bar last quarter.

A big dividend yield only tells you what a company promises to pay. Free cash flow tells you whether it can keep paying. All five names below passed that bar last year: each one paid its dividend out of cash left over after capital spending, and the best of them, Bristol Myers Squibb (NYSE:BMY | BMY Price Prediction), used only 39.3% of its 2025 free cash flow on the dividend. Below are the yield, the coverage math, the balance sheet and the one risk for each stock.
Philip Morris International: A Smoke-Free Cash Machine With a Fresh Raise

Philip Morris International (NYSE:PM) yields 3.14%. In 2025 it brought in $12.233 billion of operating cash flow and spent $1.569 billion on capex, which left $10.664 billion of free cash flow. Dividends cost $8.624 billion, or about 80.9% of free cash flow. That leaves a real buffer, though not a huge one.

The cash outlook is getting better. Management expects operating cash flow of around $13.5 billion this year, with capex of $1.4 to $1.6 billion and no share buybacks. Net debt is 2.35x adjusted EBITDA, and the company is aiming for about 2.0x by year-end. Stockholders’ equity is negative (-$6.7 billion), but that comes from years of buybacks and doesn’t signal a solvency problem.

The payout record backs this up. The quarterly dividend just rose to $1.60 from $1.47, and the payment history shows a higher rate every year since 2008. The finance chief called it an “unwavering commitment to our progressive dividend policy.”

Bull case: IQOS, plus ZYN after the FDA gave 20 ZYN variants its modified-risk authorization, gives the company smoke-free growth that funds future raises. Guidance for full-year adjusted EPS was lifted to $8.26 to $8.41.

August 18, 2026, 2:15 AM EDT. Europe’s climate losses are increasingly becoming a sovereign-finance issue because most catastrophe damage remains uninsured. Weather and climate extremes caused an estimated €822 billion of EU economic losses from 1980 through 2024, with a quarter of that damage concentrated in the final four years. Only about one-quarter of climate-linked catastrophe losses are insured. Fitch and fixed-income investors warn that recurring reconstruction bills can force harder spending trade-offs, while the EU is preparing climate-resilience and risk-sharing proposals for later this year.
